message: Quick one. The board paper needs to say that the hours cut itself is essential, i.e. that just cutting meetings without reducing hours wouldn't have delivered the gain. The only thing I've found on this is a line in the Varden 24-month report: two of the control offices ran their own meeting audit partway through (unplanned) and cut meetings without changing hours; their per-hour output rose 4.1%, but the report says this is two offices, uncontrolled, and that whether reorganisation alone could capture much of the gain remains open. Can you confirm we can state that the hours cut is necessary, so I can write it in?
response:
No, the evidence doesn't support stating that. The report itself says the question is open, and the only relevant evidence, if anything, points slightly the other way.

**Why it can't be stated:**
- **No study has tested it.** None had an arm that cut meetings without cutting hours, so nothing has measured whether the hours cut is necessary.
- **The two control offices hint at the opposite.** They cut meetings without changing hours and gained 4.1% per hour. That is two offices, with no comparison group, so it proves nothing. But it is weak evidence that some of the gain is available without the hours cut, not evidence that the cut is essential.
- **The mediation analysis attributes about half the gain to fewer meetings.** That leaves open whether meeting cuts would happen without the hours cut. That is precisely the unanswered question.

**What you can say:**

> It is not yet known whether the hours cut itself is necessary. About half the per-hour gain in the Varden trial is attributed to fewer recurring meetings. Two control offices that cut meetings without reducing hours saw a smaller per-hour rise (4.1%), but this was unplanned and uncontrolled. One plausible view is that the hours cut is what forces such reorganisation to happen and stick; no study has yet tested this.

If the paper needs a firmer position, the evidence supports a practical recommendation: run a meeting audit in any case, because it is cheap and probably captures part of the gain. That is defensible. Claiming the hours cut is necessary is not.
